ety.text: Latin satisfacerepcalq. Old French satisfierder. Middle English satisfyen English satisfy From Middle English satisfyen, satisfien, from Old French satisfiier, satisfier (also Old French satisfaire), from Latin satisfacere, from satis (“enough, sufficient”) + faciō (“to make; to do”).

senses.d: To be enough (for)
ex: That brief explanation will never satisfy.
Death shall […] with us two / Be forced to satisfy his ravenous maw.

senses.d: To meet the needs of, to fulfill the wishes or requirements of (someone).
ex: The final rehearsal of the day seemed to satisfy the director.

senses.d: To provide what is wanted or required for (something).
ex: Even three giant helpings of turkey and ham didn't satisfy her appetite.

senses.d: To pay to the extent of what is claimed or due.
ex: to satisfy a creditor

senses.d: To answer or discharge (a claim, debt, legal demand, etc.); to give compensation for.
ex: to satisfy a claim or an execution

senses.d: To cause (a sentence) to be true when the sentence is interpreted in one's universe.
ex: The complex numbers satisfy #92;existsx#58;x²#43;1#61;0.

senses.d: To convince by ascertaining; to free from doubt.
ex: The Siamese officer and the Consul having satisfied themselves of the honest intentions of the applicant, will assist him...

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French satisfaire.

Inherited from Latin satisfacere. Once the first element satis (“enough”) had been lost as an independent word, the verb was remodelled according to the Italian prefixes so- and dis-, as if derived from a Latin *sub-dis-facere. Doublet of satisfare, a borrowing from Latin.
From a- (“towards”) + contentare (“to satisfy”).
Borrowed from Latin satiāre. Compare Sicilian sazziari.

From Middle French satellite, from Latin satelles (“attendant”). Ultimately perhaps of Etruscan origin.

senses.d: A moon or other smaller body orbiting a larger one.
ex: The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.
A spent upper stage is a derelict satellite.

senses.d: A man-made apparatus designed to be placed in orbit around a celestial body, generally to relay information, data, etc. to Earth.
ex: Many telecommunication satellites orbit at 36000km above the equator.

senses.d: A country, state, office, building etc. which is under the jurisdiction, influence, or domination of another body.
An attendant on an important person; a member of someone's retinue, often in a somewhat derogatory sense; a henchman.
ex: We read in the Bible, that Nicanor the persecutor of Gods Law[…]sent his Satellites to apprehend the good old man Rasias[…].

senses.d: Satellite TV; reception of television broadcasts via services that use man-made satellite technology.
ex: Do you have satellite at your house?

senses.d: A grammatical construct that takes various forms and may encode a path of movement, a change of state, or the grammatical aspect. Examples: "a bird flew past"; "she turned on the light".
A very large array of tandemly repeating, non-coding DNA.
A community or town dependent on a larger town or city nearby.
ex: Ahead of us the lowering smoke-screen of Leeds and her gloomy satellites hung like an incubus over the land.

senses.d: To transmit by satellite.
To orbit, like a satellite

man-made apparatus designed to be placed in orbit around a celestial body

senses.d: A fulfilment of a need or desire.
The pleasure obtained by the fulfillment of one or more needs or desires; a sense of contentment with one's situation and achievements.
ex:
November 4, 1860, Henry David Thoreau, letter to Mr. D. R.
This life is not for complaint, but for satisfaction.

senses.d: The source of such gratification.

senses.d: Sexual pleasure.

From Middle French satire, from Old French, from Latin satira, from earlier satura, from lanx satura (“full dish”), from feminine of satur. Altered in Latin by influence of Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos, “satyr”), on the mistaken notion that the form is related to the Greek σατυρικὸν δράμα (saturikòn dráma, “satyr drama”).

senses.d: A literary device of writing or art which principally ridicules its subject often as an intended means of provoking or preventing change or highlighting a shortcoming in the work of another. Imitation, humor, irony, and exaggeration are often used to aid this.
A satirical work.
ex: a stinging satire of American politics.

senses.d: Severity of remark.

senses.d: Done to satisfaction; adequate or sufficient.
ex: The satisfactory results of the survey led to his promotion.

senses.d: Causing satisfaction; agreeable or pleasant; satisfying.
Making atonement for a sin; expiatory.
ex: […] therefore the ſuffering of any other nature could not bee ſo pertinent, nor kindly ſatisfactory.

senses.d: Somebody or something that meets requirements without exceeding them.
The rating given to somebody or something that meets requirements without exceeding them.
ex: I've been a good student — mostly distinguisheds and only a few satisfactories […]

senses.d: In a state of satisfaction.
ex: I'm satisfied with your progress in your homework, so you can watch television now.

senses.d: Convinced based on the available evidence.
ex: The judge was satisfied that the defendant did not go out with the intent to start a riot.
